cards.statement: In Angular v21 and later, applications use zoneless change detection by default.
cards.explanation: Angular schedules checks from framework notifications rather than relying on ZoneJS to observe asynchronous activity.

cards.statement: In a zoneless application, markForCheck waits for a ZoneJS event to schedule change detection.
cards.explanation: Calling ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck() supplies a notification that schedules change detection in a zoneless application.
cards.misconception: Zoneless markForCheck still depends on a later ZoneJS event.

cards.statement: In a zoneless application, NgZone.onStable emits after Angular finishes change detection.
cards.explanation: NgZone.onStable does not emit in a zoneless application. Code waiting on it needs a different completion signal.
cards.misconception: NgZone.onStable continues to report rendering completion in zoneless applications.

cards.statement: During server rendering, PendingTasks.run() delays serialization until its async callback completes.
cards.explanation: PendingTasks.run() registers its async callback as work that keeps the application unstable until it finishes.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, Angular selects OnPush for components whose changeDetection metadata is unset.
cards.explanation: A component with no explicit changeDetection setting uses OnPush. The strategy controls when Angular checks its subtree.

cards.statement: Changing a field of an object input by itself automatically triggers a check of an OnPush child.
cards.explanation: Angular compares input values with Object.is. An in-place edit preserves the input reference and does not itself trigger an OnPush check.
cards.misconception: Angular treats nested edits to an input object as a new input value.

cards.statement: Angular marks an OnPush component for checking when a signal value read in its template changes.
cards.explanation: A template signal read registers a dependency on that component. A changed signal value marks the component for a subsequent check.

cards.statement: Angular invokes the first ngOnChanges after ngOnInit when a component has bound inputs.
cards.explanation: During initialization, Angular invokes the first ngOnChanges before ngOnInit, letting the hook react to the initial input changes.
cards.misconception: The initialization hook precedes the first input-change hook.

cards.statement: With Eager in Angular v22, Angular's dev check passes after a checked binding changes synchronously in ngAfterViewInit.
cards.explanation: With Eager change detection, synchronously changing an already checked binding in ngAfterViewInit raises ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError in development.
cards.misconception: ngAfterViewInit is a safe place to synchronously change an already checked binding.

cards.statement: Angular runs cleanup registered on a component's injected DestroyRef when that component is destroyed.
cards.explanation: A DestroyRef injected in a component follows that component's lifetime. Its onDestroy method registers callbacks for teardown.

cards.statement: Angular executes afterNextRender callbacks during server rendering after producing the page's HTML.
cards.explanation: afterNextRender callbacks execute in the browser; Angular skips them during server rendering and build-time prerendering.
cards.misconception: Server rendering invokes afterNextRender once its HTML is ready.

cards.statement: Angular runs the write phase of afterNextRender before its read phase for layout measurements.
cards.explanation: Separating DOM writes from subsequent reads controls their order and helps avoid repeated layout work.

cards.statement: provideRouter accepts a Routes array to configure routing providers for an Angular application.
cards.explanation: Pass the route definitions to provideRouter in the application's providers so the router uses that configuration.

cards.statement: Angular ranks matching route paths by specificity before choosing an entry from the Routes array.
cards.explanation: Angular tests routes in array order and selects the first match. Place specific paths ahead of broader paths.
cards.misconception: The router sorts route definitions by specificity during matching.

cards.statement: Angular automatically sets a routed component's title input from the route's top-level title property.
cards.explanation: Angular uses the route's title property to update the browser document title when the route activates.
cards.misconception: The route title property initializes a matching component input.

cards.statement: A loadComponent loader can read its route's providers through inject() while the loader runs.
cards.explanation: The router invokes the loader in the current route's injection context, giving synchronous inject() calls access to that route's dependencies.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends eager loading for an application's primary landing pages.
cards.explanation: The loading guide recommends making primary landing pages available in the initial bundle while considering lazy loading for other pages.

cards.statement: Angular waits for a guard's Observable to complete before using its emitted navigation decision.
cards.explanation: The router uses the first value emitted by a guard's Observable and then unsubscribes, rather than waiting for completion.
cards.misconception: A guard decision stays pending until its Observable completes.

cards.statement: Angular continues looking for a matching route when a canMatch guard returns false.
cards.explanation: A false canMatch result rejects that route candidate while allowing route matching to continue with other candidates.

cards.statement: Angular activates a routed component before its ResolveFn supplies the initial resolved data.
cards.explanation: The router waits for the resolver's data before activating the route, so the component starts with its resolved data available.
cards.misconception: Initial resolvers load their data after the routed component activates.

cards.statement: Angular starts parent and child route resolvers concurrently during the same navigation.
cards.explanation: Nested route resolvers run from parent to child. Child resolvers start after the parent data resolves and can use that data.
cards.misconception: Parent and child resolver work starts in parallel.

cards.statement: withComponentInputBinding preserves an input's previous value when its matching route-state key disappears.
cards.explanation: The router sets an input to undefined when no matching route-state key exists, clearing stale values such as removed query parameters.
cards.misconception: Route input binding leaves a previous value in place when its source key disappears.

cards.statement: withComponentInputBinding uses resolved data ahead of a query parameter with the same input key.
cards.explanation: When route sources share a key, resolved data has the highest precedence for binding that key to a component input.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, Angular uses paramsInheritanceStrategy: 'always' by default for child routes.
cards.explanation: Child routes inherit parent parameters under the default 'always' strategy, including when the parent route has a component.

cards.statement: Angular reactive forms keep an explicitly created form control model in the component's class.
cards.explanation: The component creates the controls that define the form model, giving application code direct access to its value and state.

cards.statement: During change detection, NgModel synchronously applies a new bound model value to its FormControl.
cards.explanation: NgModel queues an asynchronous update when its bound component model changes, rather than immediately setting the internal FormControl.
cards.misconception: NgModel immediately updates its control while Angular checks a changed model binding.

cards.statement: Calling reset() on a FormControl created with new FormControl('Ada') restores the value 'Ada'.
cards.explanation: A FormControl initialized with 'Ada' resets to null when reset() receives no value. With nonNullable: true, it restores its initial value.
cards.misconception: FormControl keeps its initial string as the default reset value.

cards.statement: An enabled FormGroup omits disabled child controls from the value object returned by its value property.
cards.explanation: Disabling a child control removes it from an enabled group's aggregate value, so a typed group's value is Partial.

cards.statement: FormRecord supports a typed collection of controls whose property keys are chosen at runtime.
cards.explanation: FormRecord represents an open set of keys whose controls share a type, making it suitable for dynamically named controls.

cards.statement: Angular's strictly typed forms APIs apply their control-model type checks to template-driven forms.
cards.explanation: The strictly typed controls discussed in Angular's Typed Forms guide apply to reactive forms rather than template-driven forms.
cards.misconception: Strictly typed forms extend their control-model checks to template-driven forms.

cards.statement: In a zoneless application, FormControl.setValue automatically schedules component change detection.
cards.explanation: Reactive form updates change form state and emit form observables, but a zoneless application needs a separate change-detection notification.
cards.misconception: Updating a reactive form model automatically notifies zoneless change detection.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, form() creates a FieldTree whose field structure follows its writable signal model.
cards.explanation: The returned tree exposes fields by model property paths, letting code work with a field's value and state.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, [formField] keeps an input's value synchronized with its Signal Forms model field.
cards.explanation: Bind the directive to a field in the form tree. It connects the control's value changes with the corresponding signal model value.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, Signal Forms reads an HTML required attribute to add its required validation rule.
cards.explanation: Signal Forms adds required validation through the required() schema function. The form schema supplies the validation rule.
cards.misconception: An HTML required attribute registers a Signal Forms schema validator.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, failed validators stop Signal Forms submit() from running its action by default.
cards.explanation: The default submission options block the action when validators fail. Pending validators alone do not block default submission.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, Signal Forms supports a Map as a structural model container for nested fields.
cards.explanation: Signal Forms builds nested field structure from plain objects and arrays. A Map is not a supported structural container.
cards.misconception: Signal Forms expands Map entries into nested fields like plain object properties.

cards.statement: In Angular v21 and later, Angular provides HttpClient for injection through the root injector.
cards.explanation: A default application can inject HttpClient. provideHttpClient customizes its HTTP features.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, HttpClient sends requests through the fetch backend by default.
cards.explanation: Angular selects the fetch backend when HttpClient has no backend override.

cards.statement: Calling HttpClient.get() starts the request as soon as it returns its Observable.
cards.explanation: HttpClient.get() creates a request blueprint. Angular dispatches the request when code subscribes to the returned Observable.
cards.misconception: Creating a HttpClient request Observable immediately sends the request.

cards.statement: HttpClient automatically shares one backend request between subscriptions to its request Observable.
cards.explanation: HttpClient runs an independent backend request for each subscription to its request Observable.
cards.misconception: HttpClient shares one backend request among subscriptions to the same Observable.

cards.statement: Setting `observe: 'response'` makes HttpClient emit the response object, including headers.
cards.explanation: The response object exposes status, headers and body, so a subscriber can inspect more than the returned data.

cards.statement: HttpParams.set() updates the original instance that a request's params option references.
cards.explanation: HttpParams.set() returns a new HttpParams instance with the change applied. Pass that returned instance into the request.
cards.misconception: HttpParams mutation methods modify their receiver in place.

cards.statement: withXsrfConfiguration configures the names of HttpClient's XSRF cookie and request header.
cards.explanation: Pass cookieName and headerName to withXsrfConfiguration to match the application's configured XSRF token names.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends functional interceptors over DI-based interceptors.
cards.explanation: Angular recommends functional interceptors because their ordering is more predictable, especially in complex configurations.

cards.statement: When later interceptors remain, an HttpInterceptorFn's next(req) dispatches straight to the backend.
cards.explanation: The next handler passes a request forward to the next interceptor, or to the backend at the end of the chain.
cards.misconception: An interceptor's next handler skips downstream interceptors.

cards.statement: HttpClient serializes HttpContext values into outgoing request headers for the server.
cards.explanation: HttpContext stores local request metadata for interceptors. Angular does not send that metadata to the backend.
cards.misconception: HttpContext values become metadata transmitted to the backend.

cards.statement: withRequestsMadeViaParent passes requests through child interceptors before the parent's interceptors.
cards.explanation: The child HttpClient delegates into the parent's HttpClient chain after its own configured interceptors run.

cards.statement: With the fetch backend, HttpClient can emit upload progress events when reportUploadProgress is true.
cards.explanation: Browser upload progress uses withXhr(), reportUploadProgress: true and observe: 'events'. The fetch backend throws if reportUploadProgress is enabled.
cards.misconception: Enabling upload progress works with HttpClient's fetch backend.
